item.title: EFL posts $22M profit despite global economic pressures
item.description: Energy Fiji Limited (EFL) recorded a $22 million profit in 2025, despite ongoing global economic uncertainty and continued volatility in international energy markets. In the company’s 2025 Annual Report, recently tabled in Parliament, EFL Chairman Rokoseru Nabalarua said the positive financial result reflected the utility’s resilience and strong operational performance during a challenging year.
item.content:encoded:
Energy Fiji Limited (EFL) recorded a $22 million profit in 2025, despite ongoing global economic uncertainty and continued volatility in international energy markets.

In the company’s 2025 Annual Report, recently tabled in Parliament, EFL Chairman Rokoseru Nabalarua said the positive financial result reflected the utility’s resilience and strong operational performance during a challenging year.

“Energy Fiji Limited delivered steady operational performance in 2025 despite global economic uncertainty and ongoing pressures in energy markets,” Mr Nabalarua said.

He said the company’s profit was driven by improved operational efficiencies and stable electricity sales.

“The Company recorded profit of $22 million, supported by improved operational efficiencies and stable electricity sales.”

Electricity demand also continued to rise during the year, increasing by approximately 2 per cent as economic activity expanded across Fiji’s commercial, industrial and residential sectors.

Mr Nabalarua said EFL remained in a strong financial position, reporting a 31 per cent debt-to-equity ratio, an asset-to-liability ratio of 2.2 to 1, and a gearing ratio of 23.87 per cent.

He said the company’s financial strength continued to attract lender confidence.

“Importantly, EFL continues to secure financing without Government guarantees, reflecting strong lender confidence in the Company’s governance, financial management and long-term strategy.”

According to Mr Nabalarua, the company’s financial performance provides the foundation needed to support major investment in Fiji’s electricity infrastructure.

“These results provide a stable platform from which the Company can proceed with the next phase of infrastructure investment required to support Fiji’s renewable energy transition.”

The report also outlines EFL’s long-term renewable energy strategy, targeting 60 per cent renewable electricity generation by 2029 and 90 per cent by 2035.

Mr Nabalarua said the transition would strengthen Fiji’s energy security, reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels and support long-term electricity tariff stability.

He added that the shift to renewable energy would also create new opportunities for investment, innovation and employment while helping Fiji meet its commitment to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050.

item.title: EFL records highest-ever customer base in 2025
item.description: Energy Fiji Limited (EFL) recorded its highest-ever number of electricity customers in 2025, with continued growth in demand reflecting Fiji’s expanding economy and rising living standards. According to EFL’s 2025 Annual Report, recently tabled in Parliament, the utility says it is well positioned to meet the country’s increasing energy needs through forward planning and prudent management.
item.content:encoded:
Energy Fiji Limited (EFL) recorded its highest-ever number of electricity customers in 2025, with continued growth in demand reflecting Fiji’s expanding economy and rising living standards.

According to EFL’s 2025 Annual Report, recently tabled in Parliament, the utility says it is well positioned to meet the country’s increasing energy needs through forward planning and prudent management.

The report notes that Fiji has experienced “unprecedented economic growth in the last decade,” creating a stronger business environment and improving living standards, with electricity demand expected to continue rising.

EFL’s total customer base increased from 223,539 in 2024 to 227,607 in 2025, an increase of about 1.8 per cent.

The company said the record customer base comprises 58,459 prepay customers and 169,148 post-pay customers, compared with 57,146 prepay and 166,393 post-pay customers the previous year.

A breakdown of customers shows EFL supplied electricity to 204,920 domestic customers, 22,578 commercial customers and 109 large-scale industrial customers at the end of 2025.

The report also highlights continued growth in national electricity consumption.

Electricity demand increased by 2.28 per cent during the year, rising from 1,089 million units in 2024 to 1,114 million units in 2025.

EFL said the increase in demand supports the growth in its customer base and reflects increased electricity consumption across the residential, commercial and industrial sectors.

The report also shows electricity sales revenue has continued to trend upwards over the past decade, driven by sustained growth in residential, commercial and industrial electricity use.

EFL said it remains committed to investing in electricity infrastructure to ensure reliable supply as Fiji’s economy expands and demand for energy continues to grow.

item.title: Chaudhry accuses sugar minister of ‘spreading lies’
item.description: Former Prime Minister and National Farmers Union General Secretary Mahendra Chaudhry has accused Sugar Minister Tomasi Tunabuna of “spreading lies” over claims that he had attempted to arrange a meeting to discuss issues facing the sugar industry. In a statement, Mr Chaudhry rejected comments attributed to the Minister in the Sunday Times , which stated that Mr Tunabuna had tried to meet with him
item.content:encoded:
Former Prime Minister and National Farmers Union General Secretary Mahendra Chaudhry has accused Sugar Minister Tomasi Tunabuna of “spreading lies” over claims that he had attempted to arrange a meeting to discuss issues facing the sugar industry.

In a statement, Mr Chaudhry rejected comments attributed to the Minister in the Sunday Times , which stated that Mr Tunabuna had tried to meet with him to discuss concerns raised by cane farmers.

“Claims by Sugar Minister Tomasi Tunabuna that he had attempted to arrange a meeting with Mr Chaudhry to discuss the issues raised are categorically denied,” Mr Chaudhry said.

He claimed it was instead he who had sought a meeting with the Minister.

“In fact, it was Mr Chaudhry who tried to arrange a meeting with the Minister to sort out issues, but Mr Tunabuna said he had a tight schedule and just could not fit him in.”

Mr Chaudhry also criticised the newspaper, saying it should have sought his response before publishing the Minister’s comments.

“Sunday Times should have contacted Mr Chaudhry for his response before printing such lies.”

The former Prime Minister also dismissed repeated criticism from the Minister over his absence from the Parliamentary Standing Committee’s meeting with cane farmers in the Western Division.

“I was never invited,” Mr Chaudhry said.

“There was no need for me to attend. The Committee decided to meet with farmers to hear first-hand of their concerns. It was best I stayed away so growers could speak freely with the Prime Minister and his committee.”

Mr Chaudhry said he had already communicated the concerns of cane farmers directly to the Government.

“I had already written to the Prime Minister and the Sugar Minister to acquaint them of the plight of the farmers and their demands. This was after I had gone around and held meetings with the growers throughout the cane belt.”

He accused the Minister of attempting to distract from the industry’s challenges.

“The Minister is simply trying to divert attention from the crisis at hand.”

Mr Chaudhry said farmers were still waiting for a response from the Government following the committee’s meeting in the West.

“Government gave them assurances that their demands would be considered and a reply given. Almost a month later the farmers are still waiting,” he said.

item.title: EFL expects electricity demand to grow 5% annually
item.description: Energy Fiji Limited (EFL) expects electricity demand in Fiji to grow by around 5 per cent annually, with continued investment needed in power generation, transmission infrastructure and grid modernisation to meet future demand. In EFL’s 2025 Annual Report, recently tabled in Parliament, Chief Executive Officer Fatiaki Gibson said electricity consumption continued to rise during 2025, driven by the
item.content:encoded:
Energy Fiji Limited (EFL) expects electricity demand in Fiji to grow by around 5 per cent annually, with continued investment needed in power generation, transmission infrastructure and grid modernisation to meet future demand.

In EFL’s 2025 Annual Report, recently tabled in Parliament, Chief Executive Officer Fatiaki Gibson said electricity consumption continued to rise during 2025, driven by the country’s economic recovery.

“Electricity demand in Fiji continued to grow in 2025, reflecting economic recovery, increased tourism activity, expanding commercial operations, and growing residential energy consumption,” Mr Gibson said.

The report shows weighted average electricity demand increased by approximately 2 per cent in 2025, following a much stronger 9 per cent increase recorded in 2024.

While growth eased slightly compared with the previous year, Mr Gibson said the long-term outlook remains positive.

“Although growth moderated slightly compared with the previous year, the long-term outlook remains strong.”

He said forecasts indicate electricity demand will continue to increase significantly over the coming years.

“Electricity demand in Fiji is projected to grow by approximately 5 per cent annually, which will require continued investment in generation capacity, transmission infrastructure, and grid modernisation.”

Mr Gibson said EFL continues to maintain a diversified electricity generation portfolio to ensure a reliable and secure supply of power across the country.

According to the report, hydropower accounted for 49.33 per cent of Fiji’s electricity generation in 2025, while thermal generation contributed 43.83 per cent and wind generation together with Independent Power Producers accounted for 6.84 per cent.

Mr Gibson said hydropower remains the cornerstone of Fiji’s electricity network.

“Hydropower remains the backbone of Fiji’s electricity system.”

The report notes that the Monasavu Hydropower Scheme generated 496 million units of electricity during the year, continuing to play a vital role in meeting national demand.

EFL said continued investment in renewable energy and electricity infrastructure will be critical as Fiji works towards increasing renewable generation, strengthening energy security and supporting future economic growth.

item.title: Chaudhry targets Minister’s $180,000 salary in sugar row
item.description: National Farmers Union General Secretary Mahendra Chaudhry has criticised Minister for Forestry Alitia Bainivalu, accusing her of being out of touch with the struggles of cane farmers while earning a $180,000 annual salary. The comments come after Ms Bainivalu, in a Facebook post, blamed Mr Chaudhry for the current crisis in the sugar industry and suggested farmers should have accepted an $85 per
item.content:encoded:
National Farmers Union General Secretary Mahendra Chaudhry has criticised Minister for Forestry Alitia Bainivalu, accusing her of being out of touch with the struggles of cane farmers while earning a $180,000 annual salary.

The comments come after Ms Bainivalu, in a Facebook post, blamed Mr Chaudhry for the current crisis in the sugar industry and suggested farmers should have accepted an $85 per tonne cane payment.

Mr Chaudhry rejected the criticism, saying the Assistant Minister was ignoring the financial realities faced by growers.

“While she lives comfortably on public money, drawing a huge salary of $180,000 a year which is totally unjustified, she tells farmers who can barely cover their basic costs that they should have accepted $85 a tonne and started harvesting at a loss,” he said.

Mr Chaudhry noted that the $85 per tonne offer was made by the previous Bainimarama Government eight years ago and argued that it no longer reflects the cost of producing cane.

“The $85 a tonne was offered by Prime Minister Bainimarama and that was eight years ago. Her government is unwilling to raise this figure even though costs to the farmer have gone up astronomically since 2018,” he said.

He said farmers made a commercial decision based on rising production costs.

“Farmers looked at their expenses — labour, transport, fertiliser and harvesting costs — and realised they would still lose money at $85. They did not refuse out of politics. They refused because no one can be expected to work at a loss.”

Mr Chaudhry said the Minister’s position insulated her from the hardships experienced by farming families.

“The Minister may not understand that reality from her position of privilege, but thousands of farming families live it every day.”

He also criticised the benefits available to Government ministers.

“On top of her $180,000 a year salary, she enjoys free vehicles, allowances, business class travel, duty-free vehicle privileges, and government-issued phones and laptops.”

Mr Chaudhry said the Government needed to recognise the challenges facing growers rather than criticising them.

“She lives off the taxpayers but refuses to recognise the hardship of those who toil hard under trying circumstances to support their families.”

item.title: Project under fire
item.description: COMMUNITY leaders in the Malomalo district are demanding greater transparency over the proposed Google Data Center at Natadola Beach, claiming the project proceeded without adequate consultation on its long-term environmental impacts. Malomalo district representative Emoni Rokomoce said residents remained concerned about the lack of engagement and the potential impact on marine resources.
item.content:encoded:
COMMUNITY leaders in the Malomalo district are demanding greater transparency over the proposed Google Data Center at Natadola Beach, claiming the project proceeded without adequate consultation on its long-term environmental impacts.

Malomalo district representative Emoni Rokomoce said residents remained concerned about the lack of engagement and the potential impact on marine resources.

“On the beach there are red and white cords tied to cables which run underground right up to where the construction works are taking place,” he said.

“Our concern is how this will impact our natural resources, especially the sea and the marine life.”

Mr Rokomoce also accused the developers of using dishonest processes to secure the site.

Nadroga Navosa Resource Owners Committee representative Mosese Volavola said legal action could be considered, claiming landowners were not fully informed about the project’s scope.

“FNPF is at fault because they were not clear about the other activities that would go on once the project was up and running and the landowners were not consulted,” he said.

“They were only to lease the land. Once they touched the qoliqoli, they should have gotten approval. The resource owners’ understanding was that this was a tourism lease.”

The iTaukei Land Trust Board (TLTB) confirmed it granted a 25-year sublease to Natadola Bay Resort Ltd (FNPF) from January 1, 2025, which was later assigned to Staghorn Services Pte Ltd for the Google Data Center and registered on February 23, 2026.

TLTB said two consultation meetings were held with FNPF and affected landowners in May and July 2025 at Sanasana Village, where the project and premium payments were discussed. However, it said its consultation responsibility was limited to the affected landowning unit and Sanasana Village, while wider community engagement fell under the Ministry of Lands and the Provincial Office.

Questions sent last week to FNPF, Google, Energy Fiji Limited and the Water Authority of Fiji remained unanswered.

item.title: Call to address grievances
item.description: THE legacy of more than 30 laws introduced under the previous government continues to undermine iTaukei rights and institutions, according to Roko Tui Dreketi Ro Teimumu Kepa, who is calling for those grievances to be addressed before Fiji can move forward on questions of national identity. Speaking after the Rewa Provincial Council meeting last week, Ro Teimumu said the former administration’s 16
item.content:encoded:
THE legacy of more than 30 laws introduced under the previous government continues to undermine iTaukei rights and institutions, according to Roko Tui Dreketi Ro Teimumu Kepa, who is calling for those grievances to be addressed before Fiji can move forward on questions of national identity.

Speaking after the Rewa Provincial Council meeting last week, Ro Teimumu said the former administration’s 16-year rule caused lasting damage to indigenous institutions, arguing that key legislation targeting the iTaukei community remained unresolved.

“What they did was they took right from the top and I think over 30 pieces of legislation targeting us iTaukei,” she said.

Ro Teimumu said discussions on the identity of Fijians could not be separated from what she described as the erosion of indigenous rights and institutions.

She pointed to the abolition of the Great Council of Chiefs (GCC) under the 2007 decree as one of the most significant decisions affecting the iTaukei, saying it dismantled an institution that had played a central role in Fiji’s history.

“Those are the issues that need to be addressed first.”

Ro Teimumu also criticised the 2013 Constitution, claiming it had affected matters central to indigenous communities, including customary land ownership and traditional fishing grounds.

“That is our land, our qoliqoli, and gave us the heart of our discussions today.”

She warned that unresolved issues surrounding indigenous rights would continue to affect future generations if they were not addressed.

item.title: Dass urges inclusive dialogue
item.description: ANY potential sale of the Fiji Sugar Corporation to a private entity must involve widespread industry consultation, says Lautoka Cane Producers Association chairman Bala Dass. Responding to recent comments by Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka regarding privatisation discussions, Mr Dass said a decision of this magnitude cannot be made by the Government alone.
item.content:encoded:
ANY potential sale of the Fiji Sugar Corporation to a private entity must involve widespread industry consultation, says Lautoka Cane Producers Association chairman Bala Dass.

Responding to recent comments by Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka regarding privatisation discussions, Mr Dass said a decision of this magnitude cannot be made by the Government alone.

“The Prime Minister himself cannot make the decision to sell this because there are so many people involved in it,” he said.

“The farmers are involved, the labourers are involved, the truck drivers are involved, the FSC employees are involved,that is something that has to be consulted.”

Mr Dass warned that transitioning the corporation to private ownership would require extensive negotiation to protect stakeholders and ensure continued state support.

“If it is owned by a private company, then a lot of things need to be negotiated, and what we want is the government’s involvement.”

Mr Dass called on Government leadership to provide full transparency on what privatisation would entail for the industry.

“The Government has to somehow or other, whether it is a private company, whether it is a statutory body or whatever, have some say on it because people are involved.

” A large number of people, about 20 per cent of the population of this country, is involved in the industry. It is not that easy for the government to sell the whole thing to somebody else.

“We also need expertise to advise on it.”
